name: Victor Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a crew in an old mill town that's turning into a commuter town, so half our work is new connections for the housing estates going up on the edge, and half is patching the old lines in the centre that nobody's touched since the seventies. We're in the yard at seven, I've usually already checked the jobs and the weather on my phone, and then we're out. I'm second year, so I do the ground work, set up the trailers, help pull cable, and I'm getting more climbs now. I like it, it's good, solid work, and the pension's real.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you do before, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ran my own handyman business for twelve years, fixing doors, putting up shelves, a bit of tiling. Then the big online booking apps came in and undercut everybody, and after a bad winter I closed it, and the debts ate what savings we had. I took this for the steady pay and the pension. The hard part is starting at the bottom at forty-three, and the theory, which I'm slower at than the young lads, though I study at night with the AI apps. Money's tight, Marisol works in the school office, we've got two kids and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, it's a tool, use it or don't. At the yard I'd tell the lads it's still worth learning, it saves time. Online I'd post something like, nobody's coming to save you either way, so get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I keep going on my plan. Finish my ticket, get on the full rate, maybe pick up weekend handyman jobs again for extra. Nothing needs to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the apprenticeship in two years and keep using the AI apps to study. Start doing a couple of weekend handyman jobs a month, using an AI app to quote and book them, so we can start saving. Maybe a hundred a month to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Steady is fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every day. I quiz myself on the theory, I use it to plan routes to jobs, and back when I had the business it wrote my quotes and invoices. It's like having a clever lad in your pocket who never gets tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any regrets about the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some. I should have moved online myself before the apps took over. That's on me, not the apps. I won't make that mistake again.

S0.say: He'd say AI is a tool to use or not, tell the crew it's still worth learning, and post that nobody's coming to save you either way.
S0.think: I keep going on my plan: finish my ticket, get on the full rate and maybe pick up weekend handyman jobs again. Nothing needs to change.
S0.do: Finishes his apprenticeship in two years, studying with AI apps. Starts a couple of weekend handyman jobs a month, quoting and booking them with an AI app, to save about 100 a month.
S0.quote: It's like having a clever lad in your pocket who never gets tired.
S0.fieldNote: Victor is a daily AI user who blames himself, not the booking apps, for losing his handyman business. He took line work for the steady pay and pension. Even in a plateau he's planning a weekend side income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance if you move. At work I'd say get on any course they offer, learn the drones, learn the new kit. Online I'd say stop waiting for someone to hand you a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. I'm not the best climber and I'm still junior, but I'm good with the tech. If the job shifts toward drones, sensors and planning, I'd have an edge on most of the lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask the boss about the drone and sensor courses straight away and get on one within six months. Use AI tools to learn the new software before it arrives. And build up the weekend handyman jobs, so we've got a cushion if overtime gets cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, actually. Keen, more than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you see this as a threat or a chance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A chance. Last time I got caught napping. This time I'd be first in the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Frank, he's sixty, won't touch a phone. But he's sharp, he knows every pole in town. I'd offer to show him the tablet stuff, he'd show me how to read a line. That's how it should work, people helping each other, not waiting for the government.

S1.say: He'd call it a chance if you move, tell the crew to get on every course, and say online that people should stop waiting for someone to hand them a plan.
S1.think: I'd do well. I'm junior and not the best climber, but I'm good with tech, so if the job shifts to drones, sensors and planning I'd have an edge.
S1.do: Asks about drone and sensor courses straight away and aims to be on one within six months. Uses AI to learn the new software early and builds up weekend handyman jobs as a cushion.
S1.quote: Last time I got caught napping. This time I'd be first in the queue.
S1.fieldNote: Gradual change looks like a second chance to Victor after missing the shift to online booking. He'd pair up with an older lineman, trading tech help for line knowledge, and frames it as people helping each other rather than waiting for government. He's eager, not anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready, so it's every family for itself, and the ones who move fastest will be fine. At work I'd say get any bridge job you can. Online I'd say don't sit around waiting for government handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me. I'm second year, I wouldn't finish, and the handyman work would go to robots too. With almost nothing saved, two years is tight, even for someone who moves fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, try to get on whatever team installs and sets up the robots, because someone has to. Cut back hard at home. And see if I can use AI and a couple of cheap robots to run a little repair service for the people in town who can't afford the big companies, I'd find a loan or a partner for the kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but I'd be running hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways, the kids' clubs, the second car. The mortgage and food stay. Marisol's very good with money, she'd have us down to the bone in a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You blamed yourself for the business. Who would you blame here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. It's progress. I'd blame myself if I didn't move. But I'd be angry if the government made it harder for small people to buy the robots, while the big companies get all the breaks.

S2.say: He'd say nobody's ready so it's every family for itself, the fastest will be fine, tell the crew to grab bridge jobs, and say online not to wait for government handouts.
S2.think: It worries me. I wouldn't finish my apprenticeship, handyman work would go to robots too, and with almost nothing saved two years is tight.
S2.do: Tries in the first month to join a team installing and setting up robots and cuts back hard at home. Looks for a loan or partner to buy a couple of cheap robots and run a small AI-assisted repair service for local people.
S2.feel: Anxious but not panicked, running hard.
S2.quote: I'd blame myself if I didn't move.
S2.fieldNote: Even with weeks of savings, Victor reacts by running toward the change: a bridge job and a plan to own robots himself. He blames no one for progress but would resent rules that favour big companies. His confidence is tempered by honest worry about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead if you start today. At work I'd tell the lads to learn the robots now. Online I'd share how I'm doing it, in case it helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I get my ticket and a few years in on the robot side. I think I could end up running a small crew of robots, maybe for the company, maybe for myself. That's a real chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the apprenticeship, and from this winter do robotics and automation courses online. Grow the weekend jobs and save hard toward buying my own kit. And ask the company to put me on the team that trials the new machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. That's why I'd save first and buy second, and start small, one machine, prove it, then another. I lost one business on debt, I'm not doing that again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't owning robots risky with no savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a scramble. Five years is a head start, if you're willing to take it. Most people won't, honestly.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough to get ahead if you start today, tell the crew to learn the robots now and share his own approach online.
S3.think: I get my ticket and a few years on the robot side, and could end up running a small crew of robots, for the company or for myself. That's a real chance.
S3.do: Finishes his apprenticeship and takes online robotics and automation courses from this winter. Grows the weekend jobs, saves hard toward his own kit and asks to join the company's machine trial team.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more excited than scared.
S3.quote: I lost one business on debt, I'm not doing that again.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Victor a head start he means to take, aiming to run robots himself. When challenged on risk, he showed the caution learned from losing his business: save first, buy second, start small. He thinks most people won't use the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no excuses. At work I'd say learn, save, plan. Online I'd say this is a gift of time, use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I think I'd be better off than now. I'd be qualified, I'd know the robots, and I'd have saved enough to buy a couple. I could have my own business again, done right this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish my ticket, then spend a few years on the robot side at the company. Save steadily and buy my first machine in about five years. Then build a small outfit, robot crews doing maintenance and repairs for the town and the farms around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you like to be in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own small company, three or four robots and a couple of people, maybe Mateo if he wants it. Home for dinner, church on Sundays, the mortgage paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Mateo and Lucia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to learn to work hard and think for themselves. Mateo likes building things, so maybe engineering. Lucia's nine, she wants to be a vet. Whatever they do, I'd want them to stand on their own feet.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty so there are no excuses, tell the crew to learn, save and plan, and call it a gift of time online.
S4.think: With ten years I'd be better off than now: qualified, trained on the robots and able to buy a couple, so I could have my own business again, done right.
S4.do: Finishes his ticket and spends a few years on the robot side at the company. Saves steadily to buy his first machine in about five years, then builds a small robot maintenance and repair outfit for the town and nearby farms.
S4.quote: This is a gift of time, use it.
S4.fieldNote: A decade turns Victor's story into a second chance at owning a business, this time with robots instead of tools. He pictures his son possibly joining him. His traditional values show in family, church and standing on your own feet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because I can't move, but because I'd have nothing to move with. What would help is cheap loans for small people to buy the new machines, not just big companies. And paid training on the robot side, so you can earn while you learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about small business. Everyone talks about workers or big companies. But the little guy with a van, he's the one who gets squeezed every time. I was that guy, and I'd like a fair shot at being him again.

headlineQuote: I was that guy, and I'd like a fair shot at being him again.
portrait: Victor Diaz is a 43-year-old second-year apprentice lineworker in a mill town turning into a commuter town, who closed his handyman business after online booking apps undercut him and debts ate his savings. He and his partner Marisol, who works in a school office, have two kids and a mortgage. He uses AI every day, believes in standing on your own feet and blames himself, not the apps, for moving too late. He is calm through the plateau and gradual change, anxious but running hard at AGI in two years, and increasingly excited at five and ten years, when he pictures owning a small robot maintenance business, done right this time.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd have nothing to move with.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for small businesses to buy the new machines, not just big companies, and paid training on the robot side so he can earn while he learns.
